parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -acus.
Learned borrowing from New Latin -algia.
Borrowed from Late Latin -archa, from Latin -archēs, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”, “government”).

parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -izāre, borrowed from Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō), from Proto-Hellenic *-íd͏̌d͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti, from *-id- + *-yéti. Doublet of -izar.
From Latin -phagia, from Ancient Greek -φαγία (-phagía), combining form of φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”), infinitive aorist of ἐσθίω (esthíō, “to eat”).
From Latin -phagus, from Ancient Greek φάγος (phágos, “glutton”), from φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”).
From Latin -fōrmis, from fōrma (“form”), from Ancient Greek μόρφα (mórpha, “bodily form, build”). See forma.
Borrowed from Latin, from Ancient Greek γένεσῐς (génesĭs).
Learned borrowing from Latin -ismus, from Ancient Greek -ῐσμός (-ĭsmós), often already present in words taken (either via Latin, or directly) from Ancient Greek.
Learned borrowing from Latin -ista, borrowed from Ancient Greek -ῐστής (-ĭstḗs).

parole.significato: -itis (denotes diseases characterized by inflammation, itself often caused by an infection)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin -ītis, from Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis, “pertaining to”).
Inherited from Old Spanish -izar, a learned borrowing from Late Latin -izāre. Doublet of -ear, which was inherited.
From Latin -logus, from Ancient Greek -λόγος (-lógos).
From Latin -logia, from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía), from λόγος (lógos, “account, explanation, narrative”) + -ία (-ía, “-y”).
Borrowed from Late Latin -mantia, from Ancient Greek μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).
From Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).
From Latin -metria, from Ancient Greek -μετρία (-metría), from μέτρον (métron, “measurement”) + -ια (-ia, “-y: forming abstract nouns”)
Borrowed from Latin -o-.
From Latin -oīdes, from Ancient Greek -ειδής (-eidḗs).
From Latin -oīdes, from Ancient Greek -ειδής (-eidḗs).
From Latin -ōsis.
From Latin -scopium, based on Ancient Greek σκοπέω (skopéō, “look at; examine, consider”, verb).
From Latin -theca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “case, scabbard”).
Borrowed from New Latin -tomia, from Ancient Greek τομία (tomía, “cutting”), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).
Inherited from Old Spanish abad, abbat, from Latin abbātem, from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Doublet of abate.
Inherited from Old Spanish avismo, from Vulgar Latin *abīsmus, from Late Latin abyssus, from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos, “bottomless”).
Borrowed from Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion, “wormwood”). Doublet of ajenjo.

parole.significato: acacia (shrub or tree of the tribe Acacieae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acacia, from Ancient Greek ἀκακία (akakía, “thorny Egyptian tree”), from ἀκή (akḗ, “point”).
Borrowed from Latin acadēmīa.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin acadēmicus, from Ancient Greek ἀκαδημικός (akadēmikós).
Borrowed from Latin acanthus, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos).
From Latin Acanthopterygius, from Ancient Greek ἀκανθο- (akantho-) (from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos)) + πτερύγιον (pterúgion).
Borrowed from Latin acroamatĭcus, from Ancient Greek ἀκροαματικός (akroamatikós).
Borrowed from Latin acephalus, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos).
Borrowed from Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos).
Borrowed from Latin adamantem, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas). More at diamond.
Borrowed from New Latin aphēlium, from Ancient Greek ἀπό (apó, “from, away from”) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “the Sun”), modeled after apogaeum.

parole.significato: aphorism (short phrase conveying some principle or concept of thought)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós).
Borrowed from Latin agonia, from Ancient Greek ἀγωνία (agōnía).
Borrowed from Latin agoraphobia, from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá, “gathering of people or place of gathering”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).
Borrowed from New Latin agallochum, from Ancient Greek ἀγάλοχον (agálokhon), ἀγάλλοχον (agállokhon), a loanword from a Middle Eastern language.
Inherited from Old Spanish aire, ayre, from Latin āēr, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr).
Inherited from Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion). Doublet of absintio.

Borrowed from Latin alabastrum, from Ancient Greek ἀλάβαστρος (alábastros), from earlier ἀλάβαστος (alábastos, “vase made of alabaster”). This may further derive from Egyptian ꜥj-r-bꜣstjt (“vessel of the Egyptian goddess Bast”).
Borrowed from Latin alcēdinem, from Ancient Greek ἀλκυών (alkuṓn, “kingfisher”). Adapted to -ón.
Borrowed from Latin halcyōn, from Ancient Greek ἀλκυών (alkuṓn, “kingfisher”).
From Latin alectoria, from Ancient Greek ἀλέκτωρ (aléktōr, “cock”).
Borrowed from Latin allēgoria, from Ancient Greek ἀλληγορία (allēgoría, “figurative language”), from ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + ἀγορεύω (agoreúō, “to speak”).

parole.significato: allegorical (of, relating to, or containing allegory)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin allēgoricus.
Learned borrowing from Latin allēlūia.

Inherited from Old Spanish almendra (compare Ladino almendra), from Vulgar Latin *amendla, *amandula, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē), of Pre-Greek origin. Doublet of amígdala and mandorla.

From Vulgar Latin amidōnem, from Latin amylum, from Ancient Greek ἄμυλον (ámulon); influenced by words of Arabic derivation beginning al-. Compare French amidon, Greek άμυλο (ámylo), Hebrew עמילן (amilan).
Borrowed from Latin alopecia, from Ancient Greek ἀλωπεκία (alōpekía).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin amalgama (“mercury alloy”), from Ancient Greek μάλαγμα (málagma, “emollient”), from μαλάσσω (malássō, “to soften”), from μαλακός (malakós, “soft”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin amethystus, from Ancient Greek ἀμέθυστος (améthustos).
From Scientific Latin amaurōsis, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓μαύρωσῐς (ămaúrōsĭs).
Learned borrowing from Latin Amāzona, from Ancient Greek Ᾰ̓μᾰζών (Ămăzṓn).

parole.significato: ambo (a raised platform in certain churches)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ambōnem, from Ancient Greek ἄμβων (ámbōn).
Borrowed from New Latin ametropia, from Ancient Greek ἄμετρος (ámetros) + ὤψ, ὠπός (ṓps, ōpós) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).
Borrowed from Latin amiantus, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓μῐ́ᾰντος (ămĭ́ăntos).
Borrowed from Latin anabaptismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναβαπτισμός (anabaptismós).
Borrowed from Late Latin anachoreta, from Ancient Greek ἀναχωρητής (anakhōrētḗs).
Borrowed from Late Latin Anacreonticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀνακρέων (Anakréōn), Anacreon a Greek poet.
Borrowed from New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós).
Borrowed from Latin anadiplōsis, from Ancient Greek ἀναδίπλωσις (anadíplōsis).
Borrowed from Late Latin anagramma, from Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “up, back”) + γράμμα (grámma, “letter”).
Borrowed from Latin analēmma, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλημμα (análēmma).
Borrowed from Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογία (analogía, “mathematical proportion”), from ἀνάλογος (análogos, “proportionate, according to a due”).
Borrowed from Latin anapaestus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάπαιστος (anápaistos, “struck back, reversed”).

parole.significato: anarchy (the state of a society being without authorities)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin anarchia, from Ancient Greek ἀναρχία (anarkhía), from ἀν- (an-, “not”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).
Borrowed from Late Latin anathema, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνάθεμα (anáthema, “something dedicated, especially dedicated to eternal damnation”), from ἀνᾰτίθημῐ (anătíthēmĭ) + -μᾰ (-mă).
Borrowed from Late Latin anatomicus, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομικός (anatomikós), from ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “a cutting up”). See anatomía.
Inherited from Old Spanish ancla, from Latin ancora, possibly borrowed from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓́γκῡρᾰ (ắnkūră). Doublet of áncora.
Borrowed from Latin androgynus, from Ancient Greek ἀνδρόγυνος (andrógunos), from ἀνήρ (anḗr), ἀνδρός (andrós, “man”) + γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”).
Borrowed from Latin amphibius, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιος (amphíbios).
Borrowed from Latin amphibologīa, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβολος (amphíbolos, “ambiguous”).
Learned borrowing from Latin amphiprostȳlos, from Ancient Greek ἀμφι- (amphi-, “both”) + πρόστῡλος (próstūlos, “with pillars in front”), from προ- (pro-, “before, forth”) + στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”).
Borrowed from Latin amphisbaena, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίσβαινα (amphísbaina, from ἀμφίς (amphís, “on both sides”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to walk, step”), literally “going both ways”).
Borrowed from Latin amphitheātrum, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέατρον (amphithéatron). By surface analysis, anfi- + teatro.
Borrowed from Latin amphibrachys, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβραχυς (amphíbrakhus, literally “short at both ends”), from ἀμφί (amphí, “around”) + βραχύς (brakhús, “short”).
Borrowed from Latin amphimācrus, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίμακρος (amphímakros, literally “long at both ends”), from ἀμφί (amphí, “around”) + μακρός (makrós, “long”).
From estangurria, from Old Spanish estrangurria, itself borrowed from Latin stranguria, which is in itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στραγγουρία (strangouría).
Borrowed from Latin anōdynus, anōdynos, from Ancient Greek ἀνώδῠνος (anṓdŭnos, “allaying pain”).

parole.significato: anomaly (a deviation from a rule or from what is regarded as normal)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anōmalia, from Ancient Greek ἀνωμαλία (anōmalía).
Borrowed from New Latin anosmia, from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-) and ὀσμή (osmḗ, “smell”).

Borrowed from Latin antagonista, from Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνιστής (antagōnistḗs, “opponent”) (ἀντί (antí, “against”) + ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “a combatant, pleader, actor”)), from ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai, “to antagonize”).
Borrowed from New Latin anthēra, from Ancient Greek ἀνθηρά (anthērá), feminine form of ἀνθηρός (anthērós, “flowery, blooming”) from ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower, blossom”).
Borrowed from Latin antibacchius, from Ancient Greek ἀντιβάκχειος (antibákkheios).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin antichresis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίχρησις (antíkhrēsis), from ἀντί (antí) + χρῆσις (khrêsis), from χράω (khráō).
Borrowed from Latin Antichristus, from Ancient Greek ἀντίχριστος (antíkhristos), equivalent to anti- + cristo.

Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin antiphonārium (“antiphonary”), from antiphōna (“antiphon”), from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna, “responses, musical accords”). By surface analysis, antífona + -ario.
Borrowed from Latin antinomia, from Ancient Greek ἀντινομία (antinomía).
Borrowed from Latin antistrophe, from Ancient Greek ἀντιστροφή (antistrophḗ).
Borrowed from Latin antonomasia, Ancient Greek ἀντονομασία (antonomasía, “antonomasia”).
From Latin anthracītis, from Ancient Greek ἀνθρακῖτις (anthrakîtis).
Borrowed from Latin antrum, from Ancient Greek ἄντρον (ántron, “cave”).
Borrowed from Latin anthrōpophagus, from Ancient Greek ἀνθρωποφάγος (anthrōpophágos).
Borrowed from Latin antarcticus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνταρκτικός (antarktikós, “opposite the Arctic”), from ἀντί (antí, “opposed to; against”) + ἀρκτικός (arktikós, “Arctic”).
Learned borrowing from Latin antidotum, borrowed from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ντῐ́δοτος (ăntĭ́dotos), from ᾰ̓ντῐδῐ́δωμῐ (ăntĭdĭ́dōmĭ, “to give in return”) + -τος (-tos, adjectival suffix).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin antiphōna, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna, “verse response”), from ἀντίφωνος (antíphōnos, “responsive”), from ἀντί (antí, “against, in return”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”).
Borrowed from Late Latin antiphrasis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφρασις (antíphrasis).
Borrowed from Latin antipodes, from Ancient Greek ἀντίποδες (antípodes).
Borrowed from Late Latin antithesis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + θέσις (thésis, “position, stance”).
Borrowed from Latin analogus (“analogous, proportionate”), from Ancient Greek ἀνάλογος (análogos, “proportionate”), from ἀνά (aná, “on, upon”) + λόγος (lógos, “computation, reckoning”).
Borrowed from Latin anemōnē, from Ancient Greek ἀνεμώνη (anemṓnē).
Borrowed from Latin anōmalos, anōmalus, from Ancient Greek ἀνώμᾰλος (anṓmălos).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin anōnymus.
Borrowed from Latin apathīa, from Ancient Greek ἀπάθεια (apátheia), from ἀπαθής (apathḗs, “without feeling or suffering”).
Borrowed from New Latin apnoea, from the Ancient Greek ἄπνοια (ápnoia).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin apocalypsis, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ποκᾰ́λῠψις (ăpokắlŭpsis, “revelation”).
Borrowed from Latin apodīcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποδεικτικός (apodeiktikós).
Borrowed from New Latin apogaeus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόγειον (apógeion, “away from Earth”), from ἀπό (apó, “from, away from”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apologēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογητικός (apologētikós).

Borrowed from Late Latin apologia, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογία (apología, “a speech in defence”), from ἀπόλογος (apólogos, “an account, story”), from ἀπό (apó, “from, off”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech”). In the “expression of remorse” sense, a calque of English apology, and most common in Llanito, consi
Borrowed from Late Latin poplexia or Latin apoplexia, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξίᾱ (apoplēxíā), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō) to cripple by a stroke; ἀπο- (apo-, “from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”).
Borrowed from Latin apoplēcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληκτικός (apoplēktikós).
Borrowed from Latin apostasia, from Ancient Greek ἀποστασία (apostasía).
From Ecclesiastical Latin apostatāre (“to forsake one's religion, to apostatize”), from Ancient Greek ἀποστατέω (apostatéō, “stand aloof from; fall away (from the divine)”).
Borrowed from Latin apostolicus (“apostolic”), from Ancient Greek ἀποστολικός (apostolikós, “apostolic”).
Borrowed from Latin apothēca, from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē). Doublet of bodega (inherited), botica and boutique.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin apothegma, from Ancient Greek ἀπόφθεγμα (apóphthegma).
Borrowed from Latin apotheōsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποθέωσις (apothéōsis).

parole.significato: apocope (loss or omission of a sound or syllable from the end of a word)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin apocŏpe, from Ancient Greek ἀποκοπή (apokopḗ), ἀποκόπτω (apokóptō, “cut off”).

Borrowed from Late Latin apocryphus (“secret, not approved for public reading”), from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρυφος (apókruphos, “hidden, obscure”), thus "(books) of unknown authorship", from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + κρύπτω (krúptō, “to hide”).

Borrowed from New Latin apophysis, from Ancient Greek ἀπόφυσις (apóphusis, “offshoot”), from ἀπό (apó, “off, from”) + φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth”), from φύω (phúō, “to bring forth, to cause to grow”).

parole.significato: apologue (a short story with a moral, often involving talking animals or objects)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apologus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόλογος (apólogos, “story, tale, fable”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostata, from Ancient Greek ἀποστάτης (apostátēs).

Borrowed from Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “messenger, one sent forth”), from ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō, “to send off”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to set”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostrŏphe, from Ancient Greek ἀποστροφή (apostrophḗ).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostrŏphus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστροφος (apóstrophos).
Borrowed from Latin achaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἀχαιός (Akhaiós).

From Latin archi-, this stemming from Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-).

parole.significato: archimandrite (the superior of a large monastery, or group of monasteries, in the Orthodox Church)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin archimandrīta, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιμανδρίτης (arkhimandrítēs).
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin archīvum, from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon).
Inherited from Old Spanish arziella, from Latin argilla, borrowed from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓́ργῐλλος (ắrgĭllos, “white clay, potter's earth”).
Borrowed from Latin archontem, from Ancient Greek ἄρχων (árkhōn).
Borrowed from Late Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger, angel”).

parole.significato: Argos; Argive (of, from or relating to Argos)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Argīvus.
Borrowed from Latin aristolochīa, from Ancient Greek ἀριστολόχεια (aristolókheia).

Borrowed from Latin arithmētica, from Ancient Greek ἀριθμητική (τέχνη) (arithmētikḗ (tékhnē), “(art of) counting”), feminine of ἀριθμητικός (arithmētikós, “arithmetical”), from ἀριθμός (arithmós, “number, counting”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ri-dʰh₁-mó-s, form of *h₂rey- (“to count, reason”).

Borrowed from Latin arithmeticus, from Ancient Greek ἀριθμητική (τέχνη) (arithmētikḗ (tékhnē), “(art of) counting”), feminine of ἀριθμητικός (arithmētikós, “arithmetical”), from ἀριθμός (arithmós, “number, counting”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ri-dʰh₁-mó-s, form of *h₂rey- (“to count, reason”).
Borrowed from Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía, “joint, union, agreement, concord of sounds”).
Borrowed from Latin harmonicus, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονικός (harmonikós), from ἁρμονία (harmonía).
Borrowed from Late Latin arōma (“spices”), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “seasoning, spicy and/or fragrant smell”).
Borrowed from Latin harpyia, from Ancient Greek ἅρπυιᾰ (hárpuiă, literally “snatcher”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch, to seize”).

Borrowed from Latin archetypum, from Ancient Greek ἀρχέτυπον (arkhétupon, “pattern, model”), from ἀρχέτυπος (arkhétupos, “first-molded”), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “beginning, origin”) + τύπος (túpos, “model, mark, impression”).
From Latin archisynagōgus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχισυνάγωγος (arkhisunágōgos), equivalent to arqui- + sinagoga + -o.
Borrowed from Latin architectus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn).
Borrowed from Latin architectonicus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτεκτονικός (arkhitektonikós), from ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “architect”).
Borrowed from New Latin arrhythmia, from Ancient Greek ἄρρυθμος (árrhuthmos).

Borrowed from Latin arsenicum, from Ancient Greek ἀρσενικόν (arsenikón, “yellow arsenic”), identified by folk etymology with ἄρσην (ársēn, “male, manly”), but actually from Semitic source, and ultimately from an Avestan term meaning "gold". More at arsenic.
From artemisia, from Latin artemisia, from Ancient Greek ἀρτεμισία (artemisía), from Ἄρτεμις (Ártemis).
Learned borrowing from Latin artēria, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (ărtērĭ́ā).
From New Latin artēriōla, from Ancient Greek ἀρτηρία (artēría) and -ola.
Equivalent to artro- + -itis, from Late Latin arthrītis, from Ancient Greek ἀρθρῖτις (arthrîtis), from ἄρθρον (árthron, “joint”).
From Old Spanish arçobispo, from Late Latin archiepiscopus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (arkhiepískopos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”).
Borrowed from Latin asbestos, from Ancient Greek ἄσβεστος (ásbestos, “incombustible”).
Borrowed from New Latin ascus, from Ancient Greek ἀσκός (askós, “bag, sack”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ascēta, from Ancient Greek ἀσκητής (askētḗs).

From Late Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”).
Borrowed from New Latin asphyxia, from Ancient Greek ἀσφυξία (asphuxía, “stopping of the pulse”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + σφύξις (sphúxis, “pulse”).

parole.significato: asphodel (any of the flowering plants of the genus Asphodelus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin asphodelus, from Ancient Greek ἀσφόδελος (asphódelos).
Borrowed from Latin āsiānus, from Ancient Greek Ἀσιανός (Asianós). Possibly influenced by English Asian. Equivalent to Asia + -ano.
Borrowed from Latin asylum, from Ancient Greek ἄσυλον (ásulon).
From Latin Assyrius, from Ancient Greek Ἀσσύριος (Assúrios), from Ἀσσυρία (Assuría, “Assyria”) + -ιος (-ios). By surface analysis, Asiria + -io.
Borrowed from Latin āsiāticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀσιατικός (Asiatikós). By surface analysis, Asia + -tico.
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin āsthma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα (âsthma, “short-drawn breath, panting”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *escharōsus (“full of crusts or scabs, scabby”), from Late Latin eschara (“crust, scab”), from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “scab left from a burn”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin asteriscus, from Ancient Greek ἀστερίσκος (asterískos, “a little star, asterisk”), diminutive of ἀστήρ (astḗr, “star”), used in manuscripts to mark passages.
Borrowed from Latin astrum, from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron).

parole.significato: astrolabe (an astronomical and navigational instrument for gauging the altitude of the Sun and stars)

Borrowed from Latin astrologia, a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀστρολογία (astrología, “astrology”), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + -λογία (-logía, “treating of”).

parole.significato: enema (injection of fluid into the rectum)

Borrowed from Latin energīa, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia).
Borrowed from New Latin emphysēma, from Ancient Greek ἐμφύσημα (emphúsēma, “swelling, inflation”), from ἐμφυσάω (emphusáō, “to inflate”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + φυσάω (phusáō, “to blow”).
From Latin aenigma (“riddle”), from Ancient Greek αἴνιγμα (aínigma, “dark saying, riddle”).
Borrowed from Late Latin entelechīa, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia).

From Latin Epicurēus, from Ancient Greek ’Επικούρειος (’Epikoúreios), from ἐπίκουρος (epíkouros, “assisting, defending, ally”).

From Latin epigastrium, from Ancient Greek ἐπιγάστριον (epigástrion).

Borrowed from Latin epinīcium, from Ancient Greek ἐπινίκιον (epiníkion, “victory ode”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + νίκη (níkē, “victory”).
Borrowed from Latin epistolāris, from epistola (“letter”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ, “message, letter”).

Borrowed from Latin epitaphium, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιον (epitáphion, “funeral oration”), neuter form of ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “over the grave”), from ἐπί (epí, “over”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb, grave”).

Borrowed from Latin epithalamium, from Ancient Greek ἐπιθαλάμιον (epithalámion, “bridal song”), neuter form of ἐπιθαλάμιος (epithalámios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + θάλαμος (thálamos, “inner chamber, wedding chamber”).
Borrowed from Latin epōdos, from Ancient Greek ἐπῳδός (epōidós), from ἐπί (epí, “upon, over, above”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).
Borrowed from Latin epilogus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos).
Borrowed from Late Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ).

From New Latin ecchymōsis, from Ancient Greek ἐκχύμωσις (ekkhúmōsis).
From Latin echīnus, from Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos).

From Latin erōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós), from ἔρως (érōs, “sexual love, desire”).

Borrowed from Latin sca(e)na, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).
From Scientific Latin sclērodermia, from Ancient Greek σκληρόδερμος (sklēródermos, “hard-skined”) + -ia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sclērōsis, from Ancient Greek σκλήρωσις (sklḗrōsis).
From Latin scoliōsis, derived from Ancient Greek σκολίωσις (skolíōsis), from σκολιός (skoliós, “twisted”) + -sis.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scolopendra, from Ancient Greek σκολόπενδρα (skolópendra).

Borrowed from Latin scombrī (“mackerel”), from Ancient Greek σκόμβρος (skómbros).

parole.significato: school (an institution dedicated to teaching and learning)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, “spare time, leisure”, later “conversations and the knowledge gained through them during free time; the places where these conversations took place”).

From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “blade”). Doublet of espada.

parole.testo: From Latin spīra (probably borrowed), from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra).
From Scientific Latin spondylitis, from spondy̆lus (“vertebra”), from Ancient Greek σπόνδυλος (spóndulos). Equivalent to espondilo- + -itis.

Borrowed from New Latin sporangium, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed”) + ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel”).

parole.significato: a type of ulcer afflicting horses and other equids.
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin spongia (“sponge”). Doublet of esponja. Compare Galician espulla (“wart; growth in cows”), also Romanian spânz (“horse disease”).
Borrowed from Latin spādīcem, from Ancient Greek σπάδιξ (spádix).
From Latin sparagus, asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).

parole.significato: outline (a general description, a summarizing statement)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin schēma, from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma, “form, shape”).

From Latin stratēgēma, from Ancient Greek στρατήγημα (stratḗgēma).

From Latin stropha, from Ancient Greek στροφή (strophḗ, “turning”).
Borrowed from New Latin staticus, from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós).

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish estomago (“maw”), from Latin stomachus, from Ancient Greek στόμαχος (stómakhos, “gullet; stomach”), from στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin oesophagus, from Ancient Greek οἰσοφάγος (oisophágos).
Borrowed from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología), from ἔτυμον (étumon, “true sense”) + -λογία (-logía).

Borrowed from Late Latin eucharistia, from Ancient Greek εὐχαριστία (eukharistía, “thanksgiving”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin eucharisticus, from Ancient Greek εὐχαριστικός (eukharistikós). By surface analysis, eucaristía + -ico.
Borrowed from Late Latin euphōnia, from Ancient Greek εὐφωνία (euphōnía, “sweetness of voice”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound, voice”).

From Latin phalāris, from Ancient Greek φαλαρίς (phalarís).

Inherited from Latin haliaeetus, from Ancient Greek ἁλιαίετος (haliaíetos).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin, from Latin halōs, from Ancient Greek ἅλως (hálōs, “disk of the sun or moon”).
Borrowed from Latin hebdomada (“week”), from hebdomas (“seven, week”), from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás, “the number seven”), from ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”).
Borrowed from Latin hebraeus, from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos), from Aramaic עִבְרַי (ʿiḇray), from Hebrew עִבְרִי (ʿiḇrī́).
Borrowed from New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”), because the element was first observed in the solar spectrum.
From Latin heliacus, from Ancient Greek ἡλιακός (hēliakós).

parole.significato: hemina (a Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of ⁵⁄₆ Roman pound of wine, equivalent to around 0.27 L)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hēmīna (“half-sextarius”), from Ancient Greek ἡμῑ́νᾱ (hēmī́nā).
From Latin hēmisphaerium, from Ancient Greek ἡμισφαίριον (hēmisphaírion), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”).
Borrowed from Late Latin hēmistichium, from Ancient Greek ἡμιστίχιον (hēmistíkhion).
Borrowed from Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “violent bleeding”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + ῥήγνυμι (rhḗgnumi, “to break asunder, to tear, to shatter”).
Borrowed from Late Latin heptagōnus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἑπτάγωνος (heptágōnos), from ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”) + γωνίᾱ (gōníā, “corner, angle”) + -ος (-os).
From Latin hepaticus, from Ancient Greek ἡπατικός (hēpatikós, “related to the liver”), from ἧπαρ (hêpar), ἥπατος (hḗpatos).
Borrowed from Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “choice, system of principles”).
Borrowed from Latin hērōīna, from Late Ancient Greek ἡρωΐνη (hērōḯnē).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin haereticus, from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós, “able to choose”), in Ecclesiastical Greek (“heretic”), from αἱρετίζω (hairetízō, “to choose”). Doublet of hereje.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin heterogeneus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερογενής (heterogenḗs, “of different kinds”), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + γένος (génos, “kind”).

Borrowed from Late Latin heteroclitus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερόκλιτος (heteróklitos), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + κλίνω (klínō, “lean, incline”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.
From Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἑξάγωνον (hexágōnon).
Borrowed from Latin hydra, from Ancient Greek ὕδρα (húdra).
Borrowed from Latin hydrophobia, from Ancient Greek ὑδροφοβία (hudrophobía), equivalent to hidro- + -fobia.
From Late Latin hydromantia, from Ancient Greek ὑδρομαντεία (hudromanteía); corresponding to hidro- + -mancia.
Inherited from Old Spanish ydropisia, from Late Latin hydropisia, from Latin hydropisis, from Ancient Greek ὕδρωψ (húdrōps, “edema”), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”). Compare with English dropsy.
Borrowed from Latin hydraulicus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὑδραυλικός (hudraulikós), from ὕδραυλις (húdraulis, “water organ”) + -ικός (-ikós).
Learned borrowing from Latin hyaena.

Borrowed from Latin hieraticus, from Ancient Greek ἱερατικός (hieratikós), from ἱερατεία (hierateía, “priesthood”), from ἱερατεύω (hierateúō, “be a priest”), from ἱερεύς (hiereús, “priest”), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”).
From Latin hymēn, from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”).
Borrowed from Latin hymnus, from Ancient Greek ὕμνος (húmnos, “song, hymn”).
Borrowed from Late Latin hypnōticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inducing sleep, soporific”).

Borrowed from Late Latin hippocampus (“sea horse”), from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos, “sea horse, hippocamp”, from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + κάμπος (kámpos, “sea monster”)), describing a mythological creature with a horse's forepart and a fishlike hindquarter.
Borrowed from Latin hypocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκαυστον (hupókauston), from Ancient Greek ὑπό (hupó, “underneath”) + καίειν (kaíein, “to light a fire, burn”).

Borrowed from Late Latin hypocrisis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκρισις (hupókrisis, “answer, stage acting, pretense”), from ῠ̔ποκρῑ́νομαι (hŭpokrī́nomai, “to reply”), from ὑπό (hupó, “under, hypo-”) + the middle voice of κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “to separate, to judge, to decide”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos, “river horse”).
From Latin hypotheca, from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē). Compare Scottish English hypothec.
Borrowed from New Latin hypothermia, from Ancient Greek ὑπο- (hupo-, “under”) + θέρμη (thérmē, “heat”) + Latin -ia. By surface analysis, hipo- + -termia.
From Scientific Latin hypoxia, from Ancient Greek ὑπο- (hupo-), English oxygen and -ia.
From Latin hyperbaton, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβατόν (huperbatón, “overstepping”), from ὑπέρ (hupér, “over”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to go, move, walk”).
From Latin hyperbolē, from Ancient Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolḗ, “excess, exaggeration”), from ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Doublet of hipérbola.
From Ecclesiastical Latin hypocrita, from Ancient Greek ὑποκριτής (hupokritḗs, “actor, hypocrite”), from ὑποκρίνομαι (hupokrínomai, “to answer, act, feign”).
Borrowed from Latin hippodromos, from Ancient Greek ἱππόδρομος (hippódromos), from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + δρόμος (drómos, “course”).
Borrowed from Late Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument”).
Borrowed from Latin Hyrcānus.
Borrowed from Latin hȳsōpum, hyssōpum, from Ancient Greek ὕσσωπος (hússōpos), from some Semitic source. See the Greek term for more information. Cognate with English hyssop.
Borrowed from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía).
From Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós), from ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb”). See histeria.
Borrowed from Late Latin holocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὁλόκαυστος (holókaustos).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin homogeneus, from Ancient Greek ὁμογενής (homogenḗs, “of the same race, family or kind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + γένος (génos, “kind”).
Borrowed from Latin homologāre, equivalent to homólogo + -ar.
Borrowed from Latin hoplītēs m, from Ancient Greek ὁπλῑ́της (hoplī́tēs, “hoplite”).

parole.significato: hour (a time period of sixty minutes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin hōra (“hour”).
Borrowed from Latin horizontem, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn).
Inherited from Latin fōrma. Compare the borrowed doublet forma.

Inherited from an ellipsis of Late Latin pariēs fōrmācea (“a moulded wall”), from fōrmāceus, in reference to its being made by stuffing between two boards. Related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a shape, form”). Reflects pared's change of gender from the original masculine. Compare hormazo and hor
Inherited from Late Latin fōrmācium, substantivised from fōrmāceus (“made in a mould”), related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a shape, form”). Compare hormaza and horma (“dry stone wall”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin horoscopus, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκόπος (hōroskópos), from ὥρα (hṓra, “any limited time”) + σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”).
Inherited from Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”).  PIE word  *h₃órbʰos
Borrowed from Latin helīcem, from Ancient Greek ἕλῑξ (hélīx, “spiral”).
Borrowed from Latin hērōem, from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs).
From Latin hibridus, hybridus (“hybrid”, adjective), from hibrida f (“hybrid”, noun), most likely from Ancient Greek, with influence from ὕβρις (húbris).

Inherited from Old Spanish orrio, from Latin horreum, from Ancient Greek ὡρεῖον (hōreîon). The standard form in modern Spanish, with /e/ rather than /j/, appears to be the result of a latinizing modification. Compare Asturian horriu, horru and Catalan orri.
From Latin ībis, from Ancient Greek ἶβις (îbis), from Egyptian hbj.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin īconoclasta, from Ancient Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs, “breaker of images”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin īconographia, from Ancient Greek εἰκονογραφία (eikonographía), from εἰκών (eikṓn, “image, likeness”).
Learned borrowing from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”). Compare Portuguese ideia.
From Latin īdyllium, from Ancient Greek εἰδύλλιον (eidúllion), diminutive of εἶδος (eîdos, “shape, form”).
Borrowed from Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “peculiarity; idiom”).
Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).
Inherited from Old Spanish eglesia (9th century), a semi-learned descendant of Vulgar Latin eclesia, from Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “assembly”).
From assumed singular of Latin Īlōtae (attested only in the plural), from Ancient Greek Εἱλώται (Heilṓtai), plural of Εἱλώτης (Heilṓtēs, “helot”).
Borrowed from New Latin īridium, from Latin Īridem (“Iris, goddess of rainbows”), from Ancient Greek Ἶρις (Îris), due to the bright color of many of its salts; cf. also -io, element-forming suffix.
Borrowed from Latin iris, Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris).
Borrowed from Latin īrōnīa, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία (eirōneía).
Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós).
From New Latin isometria, from Ancient Greek. Equivalent to iso- + -metría.
From New Latin ischaemia, from Ancient Greek ἴσχαιμος (ískhaimos, “stoppage of blood flow”), from ῐ̓́σχω (ĭ́skhō, “to hold back, restrain; to stay, stop”) + αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”).
From Latin Isrāēlīta, from Ancient Greek Ἰσρᾱηλῑ́της (Isrāēlī́tēs).

parole.significato: isthmus (narrow strip of land connecting two larger landmasses)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin isthmus, from Ancient Greek ῐ̓σθμός (ĭsthmós, “neck”).
Borrowed from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos).
From Vulgar Latin *salma, from Latin sagma, from Ancient Greek σάγμα (ságma).
From Latin iaspis, from Ancient Greek ἴασπις (íaspis).
From earlier hierarquía, from Medieval Latin hierarchia, from Ancient Greek ἱεραρχία (hierarkhía) "rule of a high priest", from ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs) "sacred ruler, high priest".
From Jeremías, from Latin Jeremias, from Ancient Greek Ἰερεμίας (Ieremías), from Hebrew יִרְמְיָה (yirm'yá, “Jeremiah”, literally “Yahweh exalt”).

From Medieval Latin syringa, based on Latin syrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pipe, tube”) (genitive singular σῦριγγος (sûringos). The initial consonant must have passed from /s/ to /ʃ/, a sporadic sound change in Old Spanish (compare jabón).
Earlier hieroglífico, from Latin hieroglyphicus, from Ancient Greek ἱερογλυφικός (hierogluphikós). More at hieroglyph.

parole.significato: bless you, gesundheit (said after a sneeze)
parole.testo: From Latin Iēsūs, from Ancient Greek Ἰησοῦς (Iēsoûs), from Hebrew ישוע (yēšūaʿ). The exceptional use of Jesús as a first given name in Spanish-speaking countries contrasts with other historically Catholic or otherwise Christian societies. It has been linked to the widespread use of the name مُحَمَّد
Inherited from Latin sēpia. Doublet of sepia.
From silguero, from Latin sily̆bum, from Ancient Greek σίλυβον (sílubon, “thistle”).
Borrowed from Latin iota, from Ancient Greek ἰῶτα (iôta, “iota”).
Borrowed from Latin Iūdaicus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαικός (Ioudaikós, “Jewish”), from Hebrew יהודה (y'huda, “Judah”).
Borrowed from Late Latin iūdaismus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós, “Judaism”), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehuda, “Judah”).
From Latin iūdaeus (“Jewish”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehûdâ, “Judah”).
Inherited from Latin iūdaeus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), from Hebrew יהודי (Yehudi).
From Latin Iōnicus, from Ancient Greek Ἰωνικός (Iōnikós).
Borrowed from Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λαβύρινθος (labúrinthos).
Borrowed from Latin lāicus (“lay; unconsecrated”), from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós, “of the people”), from λαός (laós, “the people”). Doublet of lego.

parole.significato: lambdacism (substituting an L for another sound)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lambdacismus, from Ancient Greek λᾰβδᾰκῐσμός (lăbdăkĭsmós).

From Vulgar Latin *lotōnem, derived from Latin lotus, a borrowing from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós). Coromines & Pascual posit that the Spanish word's unvoiced /-t-/ is due to borrowing from Aragonese, presumably meaning the Pyrenean varieties that did not lenite intervocalic Latin /p t k/.
From Late Latin lecanomantia, from Ancient Greek λεκανομαντείᾱ (lekanomanteíā, “lekanomanteía”), from λεκάνη (lekánē, “dish, pan”) + -mancia.
Inherited from Old Spanish lego, from Latin lāicus, borrowed from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós). Doublet of laico.
Borrowed from Latin lemma, from Ancient Greek λῆμμα (lêmma).
Borrowed from Late Latin leopardus, from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos), from λέων (léōn, “lion”) + πάρδος (párdos, “male panther”), a later form of πάρδαλις (párdalis, “leopard”).
Borrowed from Latin lepra, from Ancient Greek λέπρα (lépra), from λεπίς (lepís, “scale”).

parole.significato: Lesbian (of, from or relating to Lesbos (island of Greece))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Lesbius, from Ancient Greek Λέσβιος (Lésbios, “of Lesbos”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin litanīa, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía, “prayer”), from λιτή (litḗ, “supplication”).
From Latin lēthargus, from Ancient Greek λήθαργος (lḗthargos).
Borrowed from Late Latin levisticum, probably an alteration of Latin ligusticum, from Ligusticus (“Ligurian”), ultimately from Ancient Greek Λίγυς (Lígus).
Inherited from Latin leōnem. Doublet of leu.

parole.significato: secondary school, high school (in some countries)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lyceum, from Ancient Greek Λύκειον (Lúkeion) (the name of a gymnasium, or athletic training facility, near Athens where Aristotle established his school), from Λύκειος ("Lycian" or "wolf-killer"). Probably influenced or derived directly from French lycée.

parole.significato: slug (gastropod mollusk without a shell or with a very small internal shell)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin līmācem, accusative of līmāx; from Ancient Greek λεῖμᾰξ (leîmăx). Compare inherited limaza.

Inherited from Old Spanish limosna, from older almosna, elemosina, from Vulgar Latin *alēmosyna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna (“alms”) (compare French aumône, Italian elemosina, Portuguese esmola), from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “pity, mercy”), from ἐλεήμων (eleḗmōn, “pitiful, merciful”).
From Latin lyncem from Ancient Greek λύγξ (lúnx).
From Latin lympha (“(clear) water”), from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē).

Inherited from Old Spanish lanterna, a learned borrowing from Latin lanterna. The change of the first vowel is explained by influence from interna (“internal”) due to light coming out of the inside of a lantern.
Learned borrowing from Latin līchen, borrowed from Ancient Greek λειχήν (leikhḗn).
From Latin lyra, from Ancient Greek λύρα (lúra).
Inherited from Old Spanish lilio, borrowed from Latin līlium. Doublet of lis. Cognate with English lily.
From the Romance/Vulgar Latin *līssius, from Ancient Greek λισσός (lissós, “smooth”). Compare Portuguese liso, French lisse, Catalan llis, Italian liscio.

Borrowed from New Latin lithium, from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”) + -io, to reflect the element's discovery in solid mineral, as opposed to potassium, discovered in plant ashes, and sodium, often found in animal blood.
Borrowed from Late Latin lītūrgia, from Ancient Greek λειτουργία (leitourgía).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin logisticus, from Ancient Greek λογιστικός (logistikós).

parole.significato: a compulsive gambler; one who exhibits problem gambling
parole.testo: From ludo + -pata, from Latin lūdus (“game; sport”) and Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).
From Latin larix, itself from Ancient Greek λάριξ (lárix).
From Latin lyricus, from Ancient Greek λυρικός (lurikós), from λύρα (lúra, “lyre”).
Borrowed from Late Latin logicus.

Inherited from Old Spanish maçiço (mid-14th c.), from a hypothetical earlier *massizo, from Vulgar Latin *massīcius, from Latin massa (“mass”), from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “barley cake”); see links for more. The sense “massif” is a semantic loan from French massif, which is cognate.
Inherited from Old Spanish madexa, from Latin mataxa, from Ancient Greek μέταξα (métaxa). Cognate to Portuguese madeixa, Italian matassa, Romanian mătase.
Borrowed from Late Latin magīa, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).
From Latin magnes or Ancient Greek μᾰ́γνης (mắgnēs).
Borrowed from Latin magus, from Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos). Cf. also mego.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin malvaviscus, from Latin malva (“mallow”) + hibiscum (“marsh mallow”), from Ancient Greek ἱβίσκος (hibískos). Cognate with English mallow, mauve, hibiscus.
Borrowed from Latin mantichōra, from Ancient Greek μαρτιχόρας (martikhóras, “man-eater; tiger”), from Old Persian 𐎶𐎼𐎫𐎡𐎹 (*martiya, “man, human being, mortal”) + 𐎧𐎺𐎠𐎼 (*χvāra, “eater”).
Borrowed from Late Latin manna, from Ancient Greek μάννα (mánna), from Hebrew מָן (mān).
Borrowed from Latin mania or Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).
Borrowed from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”). See manía.
Borrowed from Latin māchinārī (“scheme, plot”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, scheme”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. Morphological doublet of maznar, an inherited form.
From Latin margarīta, from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs).
Borrowed from New Latin marsūpiālis, from Latin marsūpium "pouch", from Ancient Greek μαρσίππιον (marsíppion). More at marsupio.
From Latin marsūpium, from Ancient Greek μαρσίππιον (marsíppion).
From Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “bread”).
From Latin mathēmaticus, from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós), from μάθημα (máthēma, “knowledge, learning”).

Inherited from Late Latin māchināre (“mill, grind”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, mill”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. Compare Italian macinare. Morphological doublet of maquinar, a borrowing from Latin.
Learned borrowing from New Latin mechanismus.
From Latin mēcōnium (“opium; excrement of a newborn child”), from Ancient Greek μηκώνιον (mēkṓnion, “poppy-juice, opium”), from μήκων (mḗkōn, “poppy”).
From Latin mēchanicus, from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin melancholia, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”).
Borrowed from Late Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós).
Borrowed from Latin melēna, from Ancient Greek μέλαινα (mélaina, “black”).
From Latin melōdia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδία (melōidía), from μέλος (mélos, “song”).

Inherited from Old Spanish membrillo, menbriello (c. 1250), from Latin melimēlum (“sweet apple”), via an intermediary Vulgar Latin *melimellum (according to Joan Coromines), from Ancient Greek μελίμηλον (melímēlon), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”). Compare Portuguese marmelo.
From Latin menta, mentha (compare Catalan menta, French menthe, Italian menta), from Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē).
From Latin Messīās.

From Latin metamorphōsis, from Ancient Greek μεταμόρφωσις (metamórphōsis), from μεταμορφόω (metamorphóō, “to transform, change, disguise”), from μετά (metá, “concerning change”) + μορφόω (morphóō, “to form”).
Borrowed from Late Latin metempsychōsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μετεμψύχωσις (metempsúkhōsis).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin meteōrum, in use as a noun from the neuter of Latin meteōrus, from Ancient Greek μετέωρος (metéōros, “lofty”).
Borrowed from Late Latin metōnymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
From Latin metopa, from Ancient Greek μετόπη (metópē).

parole.significato: metaphor (the use of a word or phrase to refer to something other than its literal meaning)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá).
Borrowed from Late Latin metathesis, from Ancient Greek μετάθεσις (metáthesis), from μετά (metá, “among”) + θέσις (thésis, “placement”).
From Latin hēmicrānia, from the Ancient Greek ἡμικρανία (hēmikranía). Doublet of hemicránea.
From Latin Mīlēsius, from Ancient Greek Μιλήσιος (Milḗsios).

parole.significato: mime, mime artist (an actor or actress who practices mime)
parole.testo: From Latin mīmus, from Ancient Greek μῖμος (mîmos).
From Latin myometrium, from Ancient Greek μῦός (mûós, “muscle”) and μήτρα (mḗtra).
From Latin myosis, from Ancient Greek μύειν (múein) + -σις (-sis).

parole.significato: myrobalan (Prunus cerasifera tree and plum-like fruit from this tree)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin myrobalanus, from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos).
Borrowed from Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρα (múrrha), of Semitic origin. Cognate with English myrrh.
From Latin myrtus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos).
Borrowed from Late Latin mȳriadem, from Ancient Greek μῡριάδος (mūriádos, “number of 10,000”), from μῡρῐ́ος (mūrĭ́os, “numberless, countless, infinite”, literally “10,000”).
Borrowed from Latin mystērium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion), from μύστης (mústēs, “one who has been initiated”).
From Late Latin mȳthologia, borrowed from Ancient Greek μῡθολογῐ́ᾱ (mūthologĭ́ā).

parole.significato: mitre (head covering of a church dignitary)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish mitra, borrowed from Latin mītra, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra).

Uncertain: * from Vulgar Latin *mōmus, from Ancient Greek Μῶμος (Mômos, “god of satire and mockery”), from μῶμος (mômos); * from an imitative Proto-Germanic root, whence Dutch mom (“mask”), German Mumme (“mask”) - see mummer. * from Old French momer (“to wear a mask”), related to momon (“mask”), fro
Borrowed from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”).
Borrowed from Late Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía).

parole.significato: monogamy (a permanent pair bond between two beings)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin monogamia, from Ancient Greek μονογαμία (monogamía), equivalent to mono- + -gamia.
From Latin monolithus (“made from a single block of stone”), from Ancient Greek μονόλιθος (monólithos, “made from a single block of stone”), equivalent to mono- + -lito.
From Latin monosyllabicus, from Ancient Greek μονοσυλλαβικός (monosullabikós), equivalent to mono- + silábico.
From Latin monosyllăbus, from Ancient Greek μονοσύλλαβος (monosúllabos), equivalent to mono- + sílaba.
Borrowed from Late Latin monasticus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin monogamus, from Ancient Greek μονόγαμος (monógamos, “marrying only once”).
Borrowed from Latin monopteros, from Ancient Greek μονόπτερος (monópteros), from μονο- (mono-, “mono-”) + πτερόν (pterón, “wing; circle of columns”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mōra, from Latin mōrum (whose plural was reanalyzed as the feminine singular), probably Ancient Greek μόρον (móron).
from Latin muraena (“sea eel, lamprey”), from Ancient Greek σμυραινα (smuraina), from σμυρος (smuros, “sea eel”).

parole.significato: a Moor (member of the Islamic people of Arab or Amazigh origin who ruled most of the Iberian Peninsula and parts of Nor…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish moro, from Latin Maurus. Doublet of Mauro.

From Latin mortiferum, derived from mors (“death”) + -fer (“-bearing, -carrying”), originally a calque of Ancient Greek θᾰνᾰτηφόρος (thănătēphóros, “deadly, lethal”, literally “death-bearing”). By surface analysis, muerte + -ífero.

parole.significato: band or group of street musicians
parole.testo: Probably from an earlier form *musga, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “of a Muse”). Compare the borrowed doublet música.
From Latin myrta (“myrtle”), from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”), from a Semitic root M-R-R meaning bitter.
From Latin mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).
From Latin museum, from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon, “seat of the Muses”), from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”).
Borrowed from Latin magicus, from Ancient Greek μαγικός (magikós), from μάγος (mágos, “wise man, mage”). See also the archaic mego, which may be a doublet. Doublet of meigo.
Borrowed from Latin machina (“a machine, engine, contrivance, device, stratagem, trick”), from Ancient Greek μαχανά (makhaná). Doublet of mashina.
Inherited from Latin marmore, ablative singular of marmor (with dissimilation), from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros, “marble”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).
Borrowed from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).

parole.significato: metric (of or relating to the metric system)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin metricus, from Ancient Greek μετρικός (metrikós).
From Latin mīmicus, from Ancient Greek μιμικός (mimikós).
Borrowed from Latin mysticus, from Ancient Greek μυστικός (mustikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin mȳthicus, from Ancient Greek μῡθικός (mūthikós).
From Latin mūsicus (“musician; pertaining to music”), from Ancient Greek μουσικός (mousikós, “musical”).
Inherited from Old Spanish nabla (1396), from Latin nabla, from Ancient Greek νάβλα (nábla, “Phoenician harp”), from ancient Hebrew נֵבֶל (nḗḇel) or a Phoenician cognate.
Inherited from Old Spanish nabla (1300), from Latin nablum, from Ancient Greek νάβλα (nábla, “Phoenician harp”), from ancient Hebrew נֵבֶל (nḗḇel) or a Phoenician cognate.

Inherited from Old Spanish nabo, from Latin nāpus (“turnip”) (compare -nip in English turnip, Catalan nap, French navet, Italian napo, Portuguese nabo, Romanian nap, Scottish English neep), from Ancient Greek νᾶπυ (nâpu, “mustard”).
From Latin naphtha, from Ancient Greek νάφθα (náphtha).
From Latin nānus (“dwarf”), from Ancient Greek νᾶνος (nânos).
From Latin narcissus, from Ancient Greek νάρκισσος (nárkissos).
Borrowed from Latin nauta, from Ancient Greek ναύτης (naútēs).
From Latin nautilus, from Ancient Greek ναυτίλος (nautílos, “nautilus, sailor”).
Borrowed from Late Latin necromantīa, from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία (nekromanteía), from νεκρός (nekrós, “dead”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”); corresponding to necro- + -mancia.
From Late Latin necrōsis, from Ancient Greek νέκρωσις (nékrōsis).
From Latin nectareus, from Ancient Greek νεκτάρεος (nektáreos), from νέκταρ (néktar, “nectar”).
Borrowed from Late Latin nephrītis, from Ancient Greek νεφρῖτις (nephrîtis).
From Old Spanish nefretico, from Latin nephrīticum, from Ancient Greek νεφριτικός (nephritikós). Equivalent to nefritis + -ico.
From Latin nēpenthes, from Ancient Greek νηπενθής (nēpenthḗs, “sorrow-banishing”) (neuter), from νη- (nē-, “not”) + πένθος (pénthos, “grief”).
From Scientific Latin pneumonitis, from Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn) + -itis.
From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breathe”).
From Latin neophytus, from Ancient Greek νεόφυτος (neóphutos).
From Latin nyctalōpia, from Ancient Greek νυκταλωπία (nuktalōpía), from νυκτάλωψ (nuktálōps). More at nictálope.
Borrowed from Latin nyctalōpem (“that cannot see in twilight, that sees only at night”), from Ancient Greek νυκτάλωψ (nuktálōps), from νύξ (núx, “night”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “sight”).
Borrowed from Latin nymphaea.
Borrowed from Late Latin nosocomīum, from Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon, “hospital”), from νόσος (nósos, “disease, illness”) + κομέω (koméō, “to take care of”).
Borrowed from Latin Notus, from Ancient Greek νότος (nótos).
Borrowed from Latin nausea, nausia, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “seasickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”).
Borrowed from Latin nauticus, from Ancient Greek ναυτικός (nautikós), from ναύτης (naútēs, “sailor”).
From Latin Nāïadem, from Ancient Greek Ναϊάς (Naïás).
From Latin nectar, from Ancient Greek νέκταρ (néktar), from Proto-Indo-European *néḱtr̥h₂, derived from the roots *neḱ- (“to perish, disappear”) and *terh₂- (“to overcome”).

Inherited from Old Spanish niéspero, néspero, from Vulgar Latin *nespirum, from Latin mespilum, borrowed from Ancient Greek μέσπιλον (méspilon), most likely of non-Indo-European origin. For the development of the stressed vowel, compare avispa (from Old Spanish biespa) and víspera (from Old Spanish
Borrowed from Latin Nomadem (“wandering shepherd of Numidia”), from Ancient Greek Νομάς (Nomás), possibly related to νομός (nomós, “pasture”).
Borrowed from Late Latin Oasis (“name of various oases”), from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”), G43-V28-G1-X1:N25.
Borrowed from Latin obeliscus, from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos).

Semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin episcopus (“overseer, bishop”) (compare Catalan bisbe, French évêque, Italian vescovo, Portuguese bispo, and ultimately English bishop), from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “one who watches over, overseer”), from ἐπί (epí, “over”) + σκοπός (skopó
Borrowed from Late Latin ochra, from Ancient Greek ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “yellow”) (modern Greek ωχρός (ochrós)).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin oda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “poem intended to be sung”), an Attic contraction of ἀοιδή (aoidḗ, “song”).
Borrowed from New Latin odontalgia, from Ancient Greek ὀδονταλγία (odontalgía, “toothache”), from ὀδών (odṓn, “tooth”) (genitive singular ὀδόντος (odóntos)) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”).
Borrowed from New Latin ophiūra (“brittle star”), from Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis, “serpent”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”) (referring to the serpent-like arms of the brittle star).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs).
From Scientific Latin oligūria, from Ancient Greek ὀλίγος (olígos, “few”) and -ūria, equivalent to oligo- + -uria.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarquia (“oligarchy”) + -ico (“-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).
Derived from Latin Olympias, from Ancient Greek Ὀλυμπιάς (Olumpiás), from Ὀλῠμπῐ́ᾱ (Olŭmpĭ́ā, “Olympia”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin onagra, from Ancient Greek ὀνάγρα (onágra).
Learned borrowing from Latin onagrus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄναγρος (ónagros, “wild ass”), from ὄνος (ónos, “ass, donkey”) + ᾰ̓́γρῐος (ắgrĭos, “wild”).
From New Latin onychomantia, from Ancient Greek ὄνυξ (ónux), ὄνῠχος (ónŭkhos) + -mancia.
From New Latin onomantia, from Ancient Greek ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”) + -mancia.
Borrowed from Late Latin onomatopoeïa, from Ancient Greek ὀνοματοποιία (onomatopoiía). More at onomatopoeia.
From Latin opium, from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion, “poppy juice, opium”), diminutive of ὀπός (opós, “juice”). Doublet of anfión.
From earlier orquestra, from Latin orchēstra, from Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρᾱ (orkhḗstrā).
Borrowed from New Latin Orchideae, Orchidaceae, an irregular formation from Latin orchis, from Ancient Greek ὄρχις (órkhis, “orchid, testicle”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin orthodoxia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía, “right opinion”). By surface analysis, ortodoxo + -ia.
Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos, “having the right opinion”).
From Latin orthographia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθογραφία (orthographía).
From Latin orthographus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθογράφος (orthográphos).
From Latin orīganum, from Ancient Greek ὅρῑ́γανον (hórī́ganon), possibly from ὄρος (óros, “mountain, hill”) + γάνος (gános, “brightness, sheen”).
From Scientific Latin otitis, from Ancient Greek ὠτός (ōtós, “ear”) + -itis.
Borrowed from Late Latin ōidium, from Ancient Greek ὠΐδιον (ōḯdion), diminutive of ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”).
From Old Spanish pavilo, from Vulgar Latin *papīlum, from Latin papȳrus. Doublet of papiro.

Inherited from Old Spanish parabla by metathesis, from Late Latin, from Latin parabola (“comparison; later, speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison; parable”). Doublet of parábola, a borrowing. Compare English parley, palaver, parable and parole.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin palanca, from Latin phalanga, from the accusative form of Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “log, trunk, body of soldiers, etc.”). Cf. Italian palanca, English plank, planch, as well as Spanish plancha, an etymological doublet.
Borrowed from Latin palaestra.
Borrowed from Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).
From Latin panacēa, Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia), from πανακής (panakḗs, “all-healing”), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) + ἄκος (ákos, “cure”).

parole.testo: From Old Spanish pandero, from at least early Medieval Latin pandōrium (“piped instrument”), after Pan, according to Isidore of Seville, from Ancient Greek Πάν (Pán). Borrowed from Latin Pantheon, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek Πάνθειον (Pántheion, “a temple of all gods”), neuter of πάνθειος (pántheios, “of or common to all gods”), from παν- (pan-, “all, everything”) + θεῖος (theîos, “of or for the gods”), from θεός (theós, “god”).

parole.significato: pope (an honorary title of the Roman Catholic bishop of Rome)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin papas, from Ancient Greek πάπας (pápas, “bishop, patriarch”), variant of πάππας (páppas, “father”).

parole.significato: papyrus (a plant in the sedge family)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros). Doublet of pabilo.
Borrowed from Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma).

Semi-learned borrowing from Latin paradoxon, from Ancient Greek παράδοξον (parádoxon). Feminine gender probably based on misinterpretation of the plural paradoxa, occurring in the title of a treatise of Cicero.
Borrowed from Late Latin paragōgē, from Ancient Greek παραγωγή (paragōgḗ, “derivation, addition”).
From Latin parallēlus, from Ancient Greek παράλληλος (parállēlos), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + ἄλληλος (állēlos, “one another”).
Borrowed from Late Latin parallēlogrammum, from Ancient Greek παραλληλόγραμμον (parallēlógrammon, “bounded by parallel lines”), from παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + γραμμή (grammḗ, “line”).
Borrowed from Latin paralyticus, from Ancient Greek παραλυτικός (paralutikós, “paralyzed”).
From Latin paranymphus, from Ancient Greek παράνυμφος (paránumphos).
Borrowed from Latin parazōnium, from Ancient Greek παραζώνιον (parazṓnion).
From Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah.
From Latin paroemia, from Ancient Greek παροιμία (paroimía, “proverb”). Compare English paroemia.
Inherited from Latin pagrus, phagrum, phager, from Ancient Greek φάγρος (phágros, “sea bream”).
From Latin parelion, from Ancient Greek παρήλιον (parḗlion), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”).
From Latin parōdia, from Ancient Greek παρῳδία (parōidía, “parody”), from παρά (pará, “besides”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

parole.significato: paroxysm (a random or sudden outburst of activity)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin paroxysmus, from Ancient Greek παροξυσμός (paroxusmós).
Borrowed from Late Latin parochia, alteration of Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “dwelling abroad”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house, dwelling”).
Borrowed from Latin Parthus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of palabra. The mathematical sense is taken from New Latin or directly from Greek.
Borrowed from New Latin parametrum (“parameter”), from Ancient Greek παρά (pará, “beside”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”); see English meter.
From Latin parasītus.
From Scientific Latin parenchyma, from Ancient Greek παρέγχυμα (parénkhuma).
Borrowed from Late Latin parenthesis (“addition of a letter to a syllable in a word”), from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin pascua, from Latin pascha (influenced by pāscuum, pāscua (“grazing; feed for animals”), the confusion aided by the end of Lent fasting at Easter), from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha, “Passover”), from Aramaic פַּסְחָא (pasḥā), from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pesaḥ).
From Vulgar Latin *pasmus, from Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm, convulsion”).
From Late Latin pasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm”). Doublet of espasmo.
Borrowed from Latin pathēticus, from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós, “sensitive”), based on πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).
Borrowed from Latin pausa.
Inherited from Latin pāvō. Doublet of pavón.

Inherited from Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”), from Middle Persian, ultimately from Sanskrit पिप्पलि (pippali, “long pepper”). Compare Catalan pebre, French poivre, Italian pepe, Occitan pebre and English pepper.
From Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós).
Uncertain. Cf. Ancient Greek πέλμα (pélma). Or a shortening of pelmazo, possibly from Latin pegma, from Ancient Greek πῆγμα (pêgma). Cf. also Romanian piemn, pielm.
Borrowed from Latin pelta, from Ancient Greek πέλτη (péltē, “shield”).
From Latin pelagicus, from Ancient Greek πελαγικός (pelagikós), from πέλαγος (pélagos, “sea”).
Inherited from Old Spanish pelicano (c. 1300), from Latin pelicānus, a variant of pelecānus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάν (pelekán, “pelican”).
Inherited from Old Spanish pena, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ).
Borrowed from Late Latin pentagōnum, from Ancient Greek πεντάγωνον (pentágōnon, “pentagon”), neuter form of πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos, “five-angled”). Equivalent to penta- + -gono.
Learned borrowing from New Latin peperomia, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”) + ὅμοιος (hómoios, “similar, like”).
Inherited from Old Spanish pepón, borrowed from Latin peponem, from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn).
Learned borrowing from Latin perca, from Ancient Greek πέρκη (pérkē, “perch”).
Inherited from Latin perdīx (“partridge”), from Ancient Greek πέρδιξ (pérdix, “partridge”).

parole.significato: parchment (material, made from a polished animal skin, used like paper for writing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish pergamino, from Late Latin *pergamīnus. Compare Portuguese pergaminho.
Borrowed from New Latin perianthium, from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “around”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

Borrowed from Late Latin peripherīa, from Ancient Greek περιφέρεια (periphéreia, “circumference, outer surface”), from περιφερής (peripherḗs, “moving around, circular, round”), from περιφέρω (periphérō, “to carry around”), from περί (perí, “around”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).
Inherited from Old Spanish cerifolio or cerfollo, with influence from perejil, from Latin caerefolium, from Ancient Greek χαιρέφυλλον (khairéphullon).

parole.significato: perihelion (the point in the elliptical orbit of a comet, planet, etc., where it is nearest to the Sun)
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin perihēlium, from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “around”) + ἥλιος (hḗlios, “the Sun”).
Borrowed from Latin periplūs, from Ancient Greek περίπλους (períplous, “circumnavigation”).
From Latin peristȳlum, from Ancient Greek περίστυλον (perístulon).
Borrowed from Late Latin peritonaeum, from Ancient Greek περιτόναιον (peritónaion).
From Latin periodicus, borrowed from Ancient Greek περιοδικός (periodikós), which combines περῐ́ (perĭ́, “about, around”) + ὁδός (hodós, “path, road”).

parole.significato: Persian (of, from, or pertaining to Persia)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Persa, Persēs, from Ancient Greek Πέρσης (Pérsēs), from Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎼𐎿 (p-a-r-s /⁠Pārsa⁠/).
Borrowed from Latin periphrasis, from Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis).
Learned borrowing from New Latin periodus, a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek περῐ́οδος (perĭ́odos, “going round in a circle, periodic recurrence”).
Borrowed from Latin peripteros, from Ancient Greek περίπτερος (perípteros).
From Latin petasus, from Ancient Greek πέτασος (pétasos).

parole.significato: petitio principii (the logical fallacy of begging the question)
parole.testo: From Latin petītiō prīncipiī (literally “an assumption from the beginning”), calque of Ancient Greek τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ αἰτεῖσθαι (tò en arkhēî aiteîsthai, “to assume from the beginning”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin petrificāre (“to petrify”), from the compounding of petra (“stone, rock”) and -ficō, a suffix from faciō (“to make”). The term petra is from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “stone, rock”); further etymology unknown.
Learned borrowing from Latin paeān, from Ancient Greek παιᾱ́ν (paiā́n, “hymn to Apollo”), from Παιᾱ́ν (Paiā́n), a Homeric god of healing, later an epithet of Apollo, from παίω (paíō, “to strike”).

parole.significato: stone (hard earthen substance that can form large rocks)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish piedra, from Latin petra, borrowed from Ancient Greek πέτρᾱ (pétrā).
Borrowed from New Latin pȳgidium, from Ancient Greek πῡγή (pūgḗ, “tail”).
Borrowed from Latin pygmaeus, from Ancient Greek Πυγμαῖος (Pugmaîos).

parole.significato: art gallery, especially one devoted to paintings
parole.testo: From Latin pinacothēca, from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē, “picture gallery”, literally “tablet box”), from πίναξ (pínax, “board, plank, tablet”) + θήκη (thḗkē, “box, chest”).
Borrowed from Latin pyra (“pyre”), from Ancient Greek πυρά (purá), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”). Cognate with English fire.

parole.significato: pirate (person who commits robbery at sea against other ships)
parole.testo: From Latin pīrāta, from Ancient Greek πειρᾱτής (peirātḗs).
From Latin Pȳrēnaeus, from Ancient Greek Πυρηναῖος (Purēnaîos).
From Latin pyrītēs, from Ancient Greek πῠρῑ́της (pŭrī́tēs).
From Late Latin pyromantīa, from Ancient Greek πυρομαντεία (puromanteía), from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr), πῠρός (pŭrós). Equivalent to piro- + -mancia.
From Latin pyropus, from Ancient Greek πυρωπός (purōpós, “fire-colored”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”).
From Latin pȳramidem, from Ancient Greek πῡραμίς (pūramís).
Borrowed from Late Latin pityriāsis, from Ancient Greek πιτυρίασις (pituríasis), from πίτυρον (píturon, “bran”).

parole.significato: Pythia (priestess presiding over the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin pȳthōnissa, from Ancient Greek Πυθία (Puthía, “Pythia”).

Inherited from Old Spanish piélago, inherited from Latin pelagus, from Ancient Greek πέλαγος (pélagos). Borrowed from New Latin placenta, from Latin placenta (“cake”), from Ancient Greek πλακόεντα (plakóenta), accusative of πλακόεις (plakóeis, “flat”).
From Latin planēta, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer, planet”), from πλανάω (planáō, “to wander”).

From Vulgar Latin *platta, *plattus, borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “wide”), because silver was often made into sheets. Learned borrowing from Latin platēa, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa, “street”). Doublet of plaza.

From Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús); this Spanish word may be semi-learned or else one that was used primarily by the upper classes in the Middle Ages (in contrast to the lower classes, who did not often use plates to eat), and hence retained a more learned character close
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin platea, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), clipping of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”). Doublet of platea. Compare Portuguese praça and French place.
Borrowed from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “to be superfluous”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin plēthōricus, from Ancient Greek πληθωρικός (plēthōrikós).
From Latin plinthus, from Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos, “brick”).
From Latin plasticus (“of molding”), from Ancient Greek πλαστικός (plastikós), from πλάσσειν (plássein, “to mold, form”).
Borrowed from Latin platanus (“plane tree”), from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos).

parole.significato: sycamore, plane (a tree belonging to the genus Platanus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin platanus, from Ancient Greek πλάτανος (plátanos).
